Well, things have been going ok in August and I am up since the start of the month, largely on the back of a major biotech rebound. Unfortunately I adjusted some exposure closing out $TEM as I continued buying $QTRX, and $CAI and $PSNL climbed upward, so missed a 9% move on a 5-6% position there on Friday. I also bought a starter in $BLLN on the mega sell off, though I do still think it is a little expensive, so just a small position.

It seems like sentiment for memory is close to all time lows. I will leave it to readers to figure out why, but it reminds me of the software sell off earlier, where vocal traders decided to invent a new narrative to fit price action. The flip from memory to optical is particularly hilarious to me as both sectors have largely delivered in line with their promises. I own $SKHY/$000660/$DRAM. I also own $AAOI. I am not sentiment about stocks like many on this platform, who treat them like sports teams, highly tied to their online identities.

The usual suspects continue to pitch 18 month narratives while trading on 1 month time horizons. I will not be fooled, personally, and continue with my goal of paying the lowest price possible for shit rather than catching a wave of sentiment.

Friday was a frustrating day, as I took a flyer on shorting some software and got wrecked. It wasn't huge, but it did have an impact on the rebound. My thinking was that $TEAM had fallen sharply out of my buying range and so I might as well short it to reduce net exposure. I promptly got wrecked. The lesson is probably that i need a slightly greedier attitude toward flipping to short on positions - i've believed $TEAM would do well in an AI world for the last 4 years. I just don't think people are turning confluence off because of ChatGPT, in fact i think it is MORE important. Companies knowledge-bases are significantly more valuable when they do not need to be mined for useful information (something the AI can do). At 9x rev, I figured whatever lets flip. But I don't think i will do that again.

I have less reservations about the $NET short which I also closed out at a decent loss. At least there I believe the valuation was indefensible from the beginning. That said, there's an argument that $NET is simply undermonetizing intentionally. The company is executing pretty hard and does look to be an AI winner. In contrast, I looked at $CRWD on Friday, and I do not get the valuation here, over 50x revenue? Completely indefensible imo.

I've noticed a lot of posters saying there's little in the market that is interesting lately, and though I've been inclined to agree, there is still plenty of stuff trading below 20x aEBITDA with >30% growth, or 30x w/ >40% growth.

Names like $APP, $CLS, $DAVE all look cheap to me on this basis after earnings. I think expectations for all 3 have been very high. But if you take $APP for example, if they trade at 18x aEBITDA and have 20% growth for at least a few more years, that is a very undervalued company if they have 75% FCF conversion and return all FCF to shareholders through buybacks. In reality, it seems they will grow significantly ABOVE 20%. So maybe this is oversold. $DRAM also looks cheap here to me. For a long time there has been a narrative that $CXMT will flood the market with cheap memory, which i've also found odd, 1) because CXMT has been selling memory for a long time, people just know the company better now post-ipo. But also 2) if memory is a commodity (the worst case scenario), why would a commodity not sell at the market price? Saudi Aramco can sell their oil profitably at like $5 a barrel because they have infinite and it takes 0 capex to get it out of the ground, but they charge the market rate because they are not stupid? I don't get this.

I also think the Chinese will simply need all their memory! ByteDance is training a 10T parameter model. TenCent is making a concerted effort to ramp up in AI. Baba's Qwen needs compute. Xiao Mi has a model. https://t.co/w5V8pj3Gm3, DeepSeek and Minimax are new emergents. Baidu is still in the game. China has 1.41 billion people, none of who are using ChatGPT or Claude. The demand long term for high quality inference in China is going to be extreme, just like with energy, where they have quite large fossil fuel production, but are still a massive net importer. There's just a lot of people in a highly developed nation.

Anyway, we will see how it all shakes out, but I don't really see the China bear case there.

Overall, it will be interesting to see what happens this week. I am still a little overweight memory, at about 10% of net. So it is tough to go crazy here even on a drop. But if we see $40 $DRAM it might be tough not to go overweight, or at least stay about 10% long memory. You can see the positions in the attached image - https://t.co/K5d1HRrxpS lets you create sleeves however you want, so thats my memory sleeve. It lets you allocate %s and multipliers too, so in the memory sleeve $KORU is counted as 3x, but since only half is memory, it's only counted as 1.5x in the memory sleeve. This helps a tonne with managing a complex long short book like mine.

In closing, I think the last thing I will try to do on Monday is get back down to 85% net exposure with slightly lower gross. I've mentioned many times this year that I need to get better at keeping this in line - if you are offside for even one day in this volatile market, you can get punished, and I have found I am not disciplined enough in making sure I hit my overall exposure goal. 93% is hardly something to panic about, but you can always act more rationally investing, and rationally I want to stay at 85% net long, so thats where I should be.

Anyway, long recap today. Good luck in the coming week, and of course, this is just a recap of my own portfolio and decisions, and not investing advice.

Heading to TomorrowX Summit 2026 in Austin, Nov 17-18. @TomorrowXSummit #tomorrowXsummit2026
If you’re also going to the event and we chat sometimes, let me know over DM and we might be able to hang at some point.

The bar is continually getting raised for what customers expect out of an investment research and portfolio tracking product. Over the last few days I have added many features to https://t.co/mOXfYvo0SO, but one that is immediately helpful for those who choose to invest in Japan is segment data and products.

ALPHAPORT SEGMENTS lets you quickly see how a companies various divisions are doing, something i've always found to be a huge PITA for Japan.

gotta say i'm surprised that Phison ($8299.TW) grew revenue 300%, 11.2xed operating profit, 34xed net income, and their July sales aren't even in the quarter (up 337%), and the stock is down 8%?

The bear case is
- they cut the dividend.
- management is concerned they will not be able to get enough NAND supply despite having favourable LTAs.
- management is heavily investing in growth businesses that may not pan out.

The bull case is
- Market cap is 15.2b USD and operating income last quarter was 819.4m USD. That gives you a 4.64x multiple on run rate earnings, with July showing further acceleration over Q2.
- Management 7xed R&D expense (all engineering) and is the leader in using NAND for AI at this point imo. Despite this, profit is up 11x.
- aiDAPTIV has been a major long term project but hasn't hit earnings
- Mediatek is going to use aiDAPTIV in dimensity phone for local AI.

Actually quite a fiddly little spot - if they told you they were just going to buy back the whole company before the end of the cycle like Sandisk, it would be simpler. But Phison's more ambitious plan might be better long term. We shall see.

My guess is Berkshire ($BRK) is going to buy one of the Sands Brothers out (or half of each). The Sands brothers own a lot of the stock (a little over 20m shares, worth about 2.6b each at $130. Robert used to be CEO). This sure looks like a cash out to me.

Not only that, I wouldn't be surprised if the large buy this morning was Weschler who I strongly believe intiated the position (see quote tweet). It would be pretty hard not to market buy there if you know Warren is about to buy a brother out at 140-150 or something (Weschler's cost basis is at least 200 i believe) and meanwhile people are market selling at $127. With 13fs coming up soon, if Weschler/Berkshire had been market buying already, they really would need to get this done before any jump in the price as well.

As a shareholder, the first thought is "am i about to get diluted?" no, this is just shares changing hands between existing owners. The problem is Berkshire should be buying the shares on the market which would make the price go up. However, as an STZ holder (unlike say, Palantir), you really want the stock price to go down as much as possible (i know, i know).

Almost no one at STZ is paid in stock. The company uses debt effectively and tries to maintain 2.5x debt/ebitda, which is pretty optimal for cannibals. The company buys back tonnes of shares. The best case scenario is a low stock price for a long time, but with great business performance. Then cash flow per share explodes. Eventually the stock must rerate (say 20 PE) and then management ideally does more dividends and less buybacks.

If Berkshire buys the 21m shares, they will own close to 20% of the company. Then Warren can leave it there to eat itself like he's done with Coca Cola. Modelo was first brewed in 1925 and is now the number 1 beer in America (which happened under the new CEO, so the transition in management has gone well). Like Coke, American Express and the Japanese Trading Companies, my read is he views this spot as +EV even if he's never allowed to sell a share again.

Moderna/Merck just ran a 1,137-patient Phase 3 trial where every single dose was unique to that patient's tumor. It worked.

The pipeline: surgical resection → whole exome + RNA sequencing → ML neoantigen ranking → mRNA encoding up to 34 patient-specific targets → manufactured and shipped in 8 weeks. One drug, different sequence for every patient.

The ML step is worth to note: the algorithm ingests WES + RNA-seq to identify somatic mutations, then predicts which of those will actually be immunogenic, ie, displayed on tumor cell surface and trigger a T-cell response. It's designed to keep learning from accumulated clinical and immunogenicity data across patients, not just per-patient.

INTerpath-001 (Stage IIB-IV resected melanoma, 2:1 randomized): combination with pembrolizumab beat Keytruda alone on both primary (RFS) and key secondary (DMFS) at interim. Phase 2b at ASCO 2026 showed 49% reduction in recurrence/death, 59% in distant metastasis/death at 5 years. Phase 3 confirmed both.

What this validates:
— tumor-specific neoantigen prediction by ML works in a blinded trial at scale
— 8-week personalized mRNA manufacturing is operationally real
— effect is additive on PD-1 blockade, not redundant

This is first positive Ph3 for individualized neoantigen therapy. First positive Ph3 for any mRNA cancer therapeutic.

What a great time to live in!!  This is the best time for AI & biotech!

Performance has been quite good this month, though I will save redoing the math until the end of the month, when I normally recalculate across accounts. Last month, I wrote about how I had attempted to “stick the landing” on the AI trade but got a little greedy with Kioxia down at ¥50,000 per share. I popped my head up for a second—went back to being a little more overweight AI—and got smacked down immediately. Oops.

That said, the general approach remained, and we ended up going into last week 35% long healthcare/biotech. This was very good positioning, with $PSNL, $TEM, and $CAI all ripping on increased interest in the sector—and then the huge $MRNA news.

This trickled down to $XGN, which seemed heavily discounted by comparison and has now rerated to +84% from my Substack write-up a few weeks ago. It still seems pretty reasonable here after last quarter’s very good execution.

I’m not sure it would be my best idea if I stack-ranked everything right now, but one thing you start to appreciate the longer you invest is a really clean story. The company has a team that consistently executed extremely well at its previous companies. It sells one product—an autoimmune blood test—and is executing well, with revenue growth and improving margins. It will add a second product. That will probably work too.

I had planned to hold $PSNL through the closing of the $TEM deal, with the dream being that $TEM would do a 50% stock swap sometime in early January 2027. Since I wanted to hold $TEM long term, this would have been extremely advantageous as a California resident. But with $PSNL trading at a significant premium to the $TEM deal price, it seemed increasingly likely that, if the deal were broken up, it would be through a knockout cash offer.

The parties supporting the deal—$TEM, $MRK, etc.—own a lot of the equity. A competing deal would have to be undeniably better, something the board would definitely get sued over if it refused, like $PARA’s massive offer for $WBD. That deal would probably be cash. So even if $PSNL went to $25 or something under a deal with a different buyer, my original reason for holding it would probably be nullified. After a lot of thought, I ended up trading from $PSNL into $BDSX.

I will write up $BDSX later, but to me it seems heavily discounted relative to the other diagnostics names. It has 82% gross margins, 35% growth, trades below 3× revenue, and is targeting a huge indication in lung disease and lung cancer. ASPs are very good. I’ll write it up on Substack sometime soon, once I have the details down cold.

Another solid winner in our “stick the landing” theme was buying a decently large position in gold. It has moved on China’s increasingly large purchases, with some follow-through after Bessent implied that he would artificially push down the long end of the curve to get rates lower. So far, the bond market has called bullshit. But Bessent is legitimately smart and will think many steps ahead, so it will be interesting to watch this one play out.

There is a lot of other stuff to comment on in the portfolio. The relative underperformance of semicap and Korean small caps seems worthy of a word or two, as does Nintendo’s bounce from the bottom. But I will leave those for the month-end write-up.

If you’re not a subscriber to my free Substack, Investing with Martin, I usually break down the portfolio’s big moves there once a month. You can see what that looks like in my last one, "June: The Turn, or The Prestige?": https://t.co/VoFM7HHDeL".

As usual, nothing here is investment advice. It is just my investing journal. But I’d be happy to answer any questions you have about my portfolio or the industries in which it is overweight.
